title: Arp 220
caption: The merging galaxy Arp 220, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Arp 220, IC 1127 · constellation Serpens Caput · about 250 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration and A. Evans (University of Virginia, Charlottesville/NRAO/Stony Brook University)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: At first glance Arp 220 looks like one strangely shaped galaxy, but it is really the aftermath of two spiral galaxies colliding. The bluish-white bright knots in this Hubble image are huge star clusters, born in a burst of star formation that the collision set off. It sits about 250 million light-years away in the constellation Serpens, the Serpent.

The crash began about 700 million years ago. It has packed roughly 200 giant star clusters into a dusty region only about 5,000 light-years across, around 5 percent of our galaxy's width. Remarkably, that small region holds as much gas as the whole Milky Way.

Arp 220 shines brightest in infrared light, making it an ultraluminous infrared galaxy. Earlier infrared observations peered through the dust and found the cores of the two original galaxies, 1,200 light-years apart. X-rays from both cores, seen by NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, point to two supermassive black holes.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.81 x 2.81 arcminutes) and distance (250 million light years), the frame spans roughly 204,000 × 204,000 light-years. Its light set out about 250 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Much of what makes Arp 220 remarkable is in infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to view this way without a telescope.

explore: Arp 220 is the brightest of the three galaxy mergers closest to Earth, and it takes its name from being number 220 in Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.
This picture was one of 59 images of merging galaxies that Hubble released for its 18th anniversary on 24 April 2008.
alt: An oddly shaped galaxy with dark dust and bluish-white bright knots of star clusters.
